articles.headline: Can’t commit to vegetarianism but want animals to suffer less? You’ve got options.
keyFacts: A Vox advice column suggested people with health issues adopt a reducetarian diet to balance animal welfare with their personal well-being.
The column cited philosophical pragmatism, which advocates balancing multiple values instead of adhering to universal moral rules about eating animals.
To lower animal suffering, the article suggested buying pasture-raised meat, choosing certified humane products, or setting specific dietary parameters.
body: Editor’s note, November 1, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary . The one below was originally published in August 2025.

This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Submit your own question here .

I typically eat vegetarian, and have considered going fully vegan out of concern for animal welfare. But lately my on-again, off-again gastrointestinal problems have been acting up, and I’ve had to go back on a more restricted diet to manage my symptoms — no spice, no garlic or onions, nothing acidic, and nothing caffeinated. Sticking to a “bland” diet is hard enough, but doing so while vegetarian is very difficult when things like tomatoes and onions and grapefruits are off the table.

I know a lot of people with these issues eat fish or meat, and some medical professionals recommend drinking chicken bone broth to soothe flare-ups. I don’t want to abandon my commitment to animal welfare while my gut sorts itself out, but my food options are limited right now. How should I approach this?
Dear Would-Be Vegetarian,

You’re not alone in finding it hard to stick to a purely vegetarian diet. Only 5 percent of American adults say they’re vegetarian or vegan . What’s more, one study found that 84 percent of people who adopt those diets actually go back to eating meat at some point. And most of them aren’t even dealing with the gastrointestinal problems you face.

So, it speaks to the depth of your moral commitment that you’re really wrestling with this. I’ll have some concrete suggestions for you in a bit, but first I want to emphasize that how you approach the question of meat-eating will depend on your underlying moral theory.

There’s a classic split in moral philosophy between deontologists and utilitarians. A deontologist is someone who thinks an action is moral if it’s fulfilling a duty — and we have universal duties like, “always treat others as ends in themselves, never as means to an end.” From that perspective, killing an animal for food would be inherently morally wrong, because you’re treating the animal as a means to an end.

Meanwhile, a utilitarian is someone who thinks that an action is moral if it produces good consequences — and behaving morally means producing the most happiness or well-being possible, or reducing the most suffering possible. Utilitarian philosophers like Peter Singer argue that we should be reducing, and ideally eliminating, the suffering that animals endure at our hands.

Deontologists and utilitarians are often pitted against each other, but they actually have one big thing in common: They both believe in a universal moral principle — whether it’s “always treat others as ends in themselves” or “always maximize happiness.”

A lot of people find that comforting, because it offers certainty about how we should act. Even if acting morally requires hard sacrifices, it’s incredibly soothing to think, “If I just do X, then I’ll know for sure that I’m being a good person!”
But these moral theories assume that all the complexity of human life can be reduced to one tidy formula. Can it, really?
Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column?
Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here!

Another school of philosophy — pragmatism — says we should be skeptical of fixed moral principles. Human life is so complicated, with many different factors at play in any ethical dilemma, so we should be pluralistic about what makes outcomes valuable instead of acting like the only thing that matters is maximizing a single value (say, happiness). And human society is always evolving, so a moral idea that makes sense in one context may no longer make sense in a different context. To a pragmatist, moral truths are contingent, not universal and unchanging.

I think one pragmatist who can really help you out is the University of Michigan’s Elizabeth Anderson. In a 2005 essay applying pragmatism to the question of eating meat , the philosopher points out that for most of human history, we couldn’t have survived and thrived without killing or exploiting animals for food, transportation, and energy. The social conditions for granting animals moral rights didn’t really exist on a mass scale until recently (although certain non-Western societies did ascribe moral worth to some animals).
“The possibility of moralizing our relations to animals (other than our pets),” Anderson writes, “has come to us only lately, and even then not to us all, and not with respect to all animal species.”

In other words, Anderson doesn’t think there’s some universal rule like “eating animals is inherently morally wrong.” It’s our social and technological circumstances that have made us more able than before to see animals as part of our moral circle . She also doesn’t believe there’s a single yardstick — like sentience or intelligence — by which we can judge how much of our moral concern an animal deserves. That’s because moral evaluation isn’t just about animals’ intrinsic capacities, but also about their relationships to us. It matters whether we’ve made them dependent on us by domesticating them, say, or whether they live independently in the wild .

It also matters whether they’re fundamentally hostile to us. Killing bedbugs? Totally fine! They may be sentient, but, Anderson writes, “We are in a permanent state of war with them, without possibility of negotiating for peace. To one-sidedly accommodate their interests…would amount to surrender.”
Anderson’s point is not that animals’ intelligence and sentience don’t matter. It’s that lots of other things matter, too, including our own ability to thrive.

With this pragmatic approach in mind, you can consider how to balance your concern for animal welfare with your concern for your own welfare. Instead of thinking in terms of a moral absolute that would force you into a “purist” diet no matter the cost to you, you can consider a “reducetarian” diet, which allows you to ease your own struggle while also taking care for animals seriously.
The key thing to realize is that some types of animal consumption cause a lot less suffering than others.

For one thing, if you’re eating meat, try to buy the pasture-raised kind and not the kind that comes from factory farms — the huge industrialized facilities that supply 99 percent of America’s meat . In these facilities, animals are tightly packed together and live under unbelievably harsh and unsanitary conditions. They’re also often mutilated without pain relief : think pigs being castrated, cows being dehorned, and hens being debeaked. Oh, and chickens have been bred to be so big that they’re in constant pain ; they live miserable lives from start to finish.

A pasture-raised label doesn’t mean an animal has been spared all of the harms of modern agriculture — it doesn’t guarantee that pain relief is used for painful procedures, and farm animals across different production systems have been bred to maximize production, which can take a toll on their welfare. And of course they’ll ultimately meet the same fate as those raised on factory farms — slaughter. But your goal here is to meaningfully reduce, not 100 percent eliminate, the harms. And at least pasture-raised animals have gotten to roam around in a field and engage in natural behaviors up until the end.

It’s a similar story for fish, by the way. More than half of the fish we eat comes from fish farms, which are basically just underwater factory farms. Wild-caught fish is not perfect — slow, suffocating deaths are common — but it’s better than farmed.

The caveat here is that a lot of the welfare labels you’ll see on animal products are basically a con . And some certification schemes have similar names, so you have to pay close attention. If you see the label “Certified Humane,” that’s genuinely higher-welfare — but don’t mistake it for “American Humane Certified,” which is really not. And be wary of putting much stock in labels like “cage-free” or “free-range.” They’re better than nothing, but because the terms are often ill-defined and unenforced, they’re not as meaningful as you might think. Here’s a good guide to separating the real deal from the advertising spin.

Another classic recommendation among animal welfare advocates is to eat bigger animals — in other words, go for beef rather than chicken. That’s both because of how miserable chickens’ lives are on factory farms and because, as my former colleague Kelsey Piper has written , it just takes way more chicken lives than cow lives to feed people. Cows are huge, producing about 500 pounds of beef apiece, while a chicken yields only a few pounds of meat. So, every year, the average American eats about 23 chickens and just over one-tenth of one cow .

That said, cows take a heavier toll on the climate than chickens do, so you don’t want to eat tons of beef either. The environment is also one of the key values at stake in our consumption choices, so that has to factor in, too.

Of course, another possibility — to the extent that this works with your gastrointestinal issues — is to reach for low-fiber plant-based foods like tofu, seitan, and the smorgasbord of newer products now available (like Beyond and Impossible burgers).

But assuming you’re going to eat meat, it’s a good idea to set some clear parameters and standards around your reducetarian diet. A lot of reducetarians — myself included — have fallen into the trap of saying, “I’ll reduce how much meat I eat,” but forgetting to quantify what that means. That can lead you to eat more meat than you’d intended. So it’s probably better to commit to something like “weekday vegetarian” or “vegan before six” — you can check out the Reducetarian Foundation for suggestions.

At the end of the day, remember that there’s a plurality of values at stake here, and no one of them necessarily trumps all the others. If you feel that eating some meat is important for your well-being right now, and you try to do that in ways that keep suffering for animals to a minimum, I don’t think you need to feel bad about that. That’s because you won’t be shirking your values: You’ll be recognizing that your values are plural, and you’re doing your best to balance between them. That may be the best any of us can really do.
Bonus: What I’m reading

The blogger Bentham’s Bulldog published a piece titled “ How to cause less suffering while eating animals .” It contains some of the same recommendations I mentioned above, but the underlying ethical framework is different and it makes one recommendation I didn’t: “offsetting” your meat consumption by donating to highly effective animal charities . I worry that offsetting might create a moral hazard, as with people offsetting their carbon emissions and then potentially feeling free to fly more. But it’s worth considering, particularly if you pair it with clear parameters around your reducetarian diet.

This Aeon essay answers a question I’ve often wondered about: Why haven’t other animals — say, birds — developed complex civilizations like we humans have? Why don’t they build rocket ships, argue about economic policy, and play canasta? I’m grateful to the evolutionary biologist who wrote this piece for finally giving me a satisfying answer.

I can’t stop thinking about this post on how AI companies may have designed chatbots to play an underspecified “helpful assistant” character who, due to being underspecified, looks to the internet for examples of how to play that role, finds tons of science fiction about cheesy robots, and thus starts to behave like a cheesy sci-fi robot (ChatGPT will say things like, “Gee, that really tickles my circuits!”). This post is mega-long, deeply trippy, and worth reading.

articles.headline: The Proud Boys Are Infiltrating DSA Meetings
keyFacts: Around 50 Proud Boys gathered outside a North Carolina library, with five entering a Democratic Socialists of America meeting inside.
The Proud Boys are targeting the Democratic Socialists of America, claiming the growing socialist group poses a threat to the country.
A DSA representative stated that the organization aims to pass policies and amend the Constitution through democratic processes, not violence.
body: WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. — Two Proud Boys conducted overwatch from a parking garage. Another flew a drone overhead. Below, at the Central Library here in North Carolina, around 50 Proud Boys from chapters around the country had gathered to oppose the Democratic Socialists of America, who were meeting inside.

The Proud Boys had scouted the location, putting together a five-paragraph field order that included the entrances and exits, communication channels, and medical plans. They had leaked news that they would be attending so supporters of the DSA would show up. Some, inspired by claims — which seem to be completely unfounded — that wealthy leftists had been funding a left-wing “street army” to fight for socialism, wanted to see if the Proud Boys’ presence would bring them to town.

Dressed in their signature black and yellow twin-tipped Fred Perry polo shirts, some with masks pulled up to cover their faces, the men traded insults and curses, alongside some conversation, with counterprotesters on the sun-dappled sidewalk. The police arrived and stayed to observe but made no arrests.
Five of the Proud Boys eventually entered the building, making their way to the meeting in the library’s auditorium.

“They tried to block us from the first entrance. We got through there. [Then] they tried to block us from the second entrance,” said a Cape Fear Proud Boys member known as “Johnny Ringo.” (Many Proud Boys use pseudonyms like this within their chapters and with the press.)

At the check-in table at the library, one Proud Boy took a name tag and scrawled “Felon” on it. He wandered over to the DSA snack area, where he and “S. Laughter,” a Proud Boy from Florida, ate most of the pumpkin spice doughnut holes and mini muffins on offer.
“You claim to be against socialism, and yet you eat our free food,” quipped Evelyn Allen, co-chair of the chapter.
“See what happens?” Laughter said. “A strong man comes in and takes all the food, and then you’ve got to wait in line — just like real socialism!”

Years after the street brawls of 2020 and members’ seditious conspiracy convictions connected to the Jan. 6 insurrection at the U.S. Capitol cemented their notorious reputation, the far-right Proud Boys have a new campaign: targeting the DSA, which they see as a threat to the American way of life.
The highly active Cape Fear chapter is leading the charge, as the Proud Boys set out to expose what they say are the Marxist ambitions and violence inherent in socialism.

“The DSA people, the far left, are way more comfortable with violence than we are,” Ringo said. (According to the Prosecution Project, maintained by researchers at the University of Cincinnati, there have been 1,086 cases of political violence based on leftist ideological affiliations, compared to 3,114 for rightists since 1990. Outside of the Jan. 6 insurrection, 18 cases are linked to Proud Boys, and none are linked to the DSA or socialism; NPR’s Jan. 6 Archive lists dozens of Proud Boys, who have since been pardoned, who were charged for their roles in the Capitol riot.)

Despite the evidence to the contrary, rhetoric about left-wing violence has taken off — and has been recently amplified by a right-wing influencer who alleges that groups across the left, from the DSA to No Kings protesters, are engaged in a complex, violent plot to shift power into the hands of Democratic governors after the midterm elections. The Proud Boys also point to websites for groups like the Marxist Unity Group, a caucus within the DSA recognized by multiple chapters that describes itself as a “faction” of the DSA. While MUG advocates for policy in DSA rather than dictating its official platform, MUG calls for a socialist revolution through a democratic mandate while acknowledging that the working class will need to be armed to resist those who oppose the change.

Meanwhile, the DSA is rising in national prominence. One-third of Democrats now identify as democratic socialists. DSA members in office, like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.), have high approval ratings among their constituents, advocating for policies that are popular with the general public, including universal healthcare, taxing the rich and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

As democratic socialism gains political power, the Proud Boys are positioning it as the latest boogeyman — and see their pushback on the DSA as a way to reassert their place in the American political landscape. The DSA’s indifference to their provocations has kept the Proud Boys’ campaign pretty low-key, but the group’s unwillingness to back down, combined with what seems to be a genuine belief that the people on the other side are violent, dangerous or unstable, means that political violence can be just below the surface.
“Yes, we’ve been quiet, but you know what? We can show up in numbers if we need to,” said a North Carolina Proud Boy called “Beast Mode.”

On a table in the library, the Proud Boys found pamphlets titled “An Antifascist Guide to the Proud Boys” that the DSA had made in anticipation of the event. It describes them as a far-right extremist group with a history of using violence, targeted harassment and intimidation to reach their goals, noting the high rate of arrests for extremist activities in the group. One page, which describes the process for rising through the ranks of the Proud Boys, is titled “The Ladder to Loserdom.” Ringo scrawled “CAPE FEAR WAS HERE!” in black marker across the top of one pamphlet and brought another home with him.

Some Proud Boys lurked in the back of the room, arms crossed, listening to the meeting, which went on as though they weren’t there. Others, trying to film the speakers, maneuvered around members who tried to block their view with rainbow umbrellas. They were treated to updates from the Queer Socialists Caucus and the Socialist Politics in Office Committee, along with the Mutual Aid Committee’s discussion of its Free Fridge Project, which gives away food to those in need. One member described it as one of the group’s more boring meetings.
The Proud Boys believe that more sinister plans lurk beneath the dull agenda, and that the DSA’s mild appearance and pro-social projects mask something darker.

They point to the Program for the national DSA, a document that states its positions and vision for where the country should go. It includes a call to expand the House of Representatives, abolish the Senate, and replace the president and Supreme Court with an executive and judiciary chosen by Congress. These goals would require a new or substantially changed Constitution, and the Proud Boys argue the DSA intends to achieve that, eventually, with violence.
“They’re not talking about a … constitutional convention. They’re not talking about ratifying new amendments,” Ringo said. “How else does that happen?”

“Our fight with the DSA is a push to have opposition now, early, before it metastasizes,” he said. “The Bolsheviks famously had a small percentage of the overall Russian population and ushered in the Soviet Union. It doesn’t take much.”

The national DSA did not respond to a request for comment. But Khaet Grindell, the communications coordinator for the Piedmont Triad DSA, pushed back on the Proud Boys’ interpretation of the organization’s mission.

“The whole point of DSA candidates running for office and winning elections is to pass our policies and (eventually) amend the Constitution — democratically,” she said. “If … they want to scare people because we want universal healthcare, they’re going to be hard-pressed to find a good audience for that message.”

The DSA has, indeed, been popular with voters in the current election cycle. The organization has endorsed 131 candidates in 30 states, and its candidates defeated some long-term incumbents in the primaries. In New York, for example, all of the candidates Mamdani endorsed for Congress won their Democratic primaries, including DSA members Claire Valdez, Brad Lander and Darializa Avila Chevalier, who unseated five-term Rep. Adriano Espaillat. Their platforms largely center on issues related to affordability, workers’ rights, expanding public services and reducing corporate influence in government. Although the DSA’s national program calls for sweeping changes to American capitalism, its congressional candidates have generally emphasized more immediate issues, especially housing, energy and healthcare costs.

And while the national DSA platform does call for changes that would rise to a constitutional level, it is generally focused on expanding democratic control. The Program explicitly calls for multiparty elections, proportional representation, ranked-choice voting and publicly financed elections.

Outside the library, as the afternoon wound down and the Proud Boys dispersed, a woman in jeans, a red tank top and a mask followed one group toward the parking garage. She was not a member of the DSA, according to the local chapter. As they walked, she reached into her black purse. The Proud Boys said it looked like she was implying she had a gun.
“Honestly, it’s probably the one of the times I’ve been in fear for my life,” Beast Mode said.

She followed the Proud Boys into the garage, where there was a tense standoff, according to video of the incident HuffPost has reviewed. The Proud Boys warned her that she was putting herself in a dangerous situation. She stood steadfast, filming them and eventually calling the police, until the Proud Boys left.
“That became a very dangerous situation,” Laughter said. If she pulled a gun, he mused, the Proud Boys would have pulled theirs, too. “That could have been very bad.”

There was no violence at the library that day, but the interaction highlights a risk that the Proud Boys bring to events. While many chapters these days tend to be fastidious about the law and avoiding arrest, they also pride themselves on not backing down from a fight.
“We’re not going to start anything,” said Beast Mode, “but we’ll gladly finish it.”
“When things do happen,” said Laughter, “we make self-defense look like assault.”

Earlier this summer, the Proud Boys intervened in another DSA project. In Wilmington, North Carolina, the local DSA chapter had been building benches and placing them at bus stops so community members would have a place to sit. Some of the multicolored benches were painted with messages like “Liberation for all!,” “Everything for Everyone” and “No Rent for Slumlords” alongside paintings of animals, flowers and buildings.

The Proud Boys nabbed two benches from the bus stops, took them to an undisclosed location in the woods, and repainted them in their signature black and yellow. One bench is decorated with yellow stars on the black seat and has “Proud Boys” written across the back. Another that reads “Socialism is Slavery” was briefly returned to a bus stop for a photo that the Proud Boys posted on their Telegram channel.
Then Dane Scalise, the Republican vice chair of the county commissioners, stepped in.

“The Democrat Socialists of America (DSA) has spent over a year placing unauthorized, non-compliant benches painted with political propaganda,” he wrote on X. “I will not abide further lawlessness or calls for vigilantism by the DSA, the Proud Boys, or anyone else. ... These benches will be removed. Law and order will be restored.”

The DSA’s benches were quickly cleared from all the bus stops and put in storage. The two benches the Proud Boys took now decorate their clubhouse deep in the Carolina swamp. The bus stops where the benches once stood still have no seating.
“If it stops socialist propaganda from being plastered all over town, that’s a tradeoff I’m willing to make,” Ringo said.

Madison Morrison, a Wilmington resident who identifies as a socialist but is not a member of the DSA, sees the Proud Boys’ bench panting as a stunt designed to gain visibility through the DSA’s successes.“They would be more intimidating if they had thoughts of their own,” she said. The Wilmington DSA declined repeated requests for an interview.

On a crisp fall Sunday morning under a Carolina blue sky, the DSA’s work continued. In Wilmington, the chapter held a Halloween costume and coat swap at the LGBTQ Center’s Family Pride Day. In Winston-Salem, more than a dozen members of the Piedmont Triad DSA gathered outside Mothership Studios. Beside a mural reading “ICE melts fast in the South,” they cleaned up and restocked a wood shed that housed the group’s Free Fridge and a food pantry. Canned goods, baking supplies, loaves of bread and fruit snacks lined the shelves alongside the refrigerator stocked with eggs, fresh fruit and vegetables, yogurt, and fresh pasta. Members spoke warmly with one another about their ongoing projects before dispersing for a meeting of the chapter’s book club.

“Socialism has never been more popular — in the polls and elsewhere,” said Grindell, the communications coordinator. “We have our own projects and our own work that we spend our time on. Thinking of ourselves in relation to this group of losers is not something I even considered before they decided to show up to our meeting.”
“The Proud Boys think about the DSA more than the DSA thinks about the Proud Boys. Have you seen ‘Mean Girls’?” she asked. “It’s like, ’Why are you so obsessed with me?’”

articles.headline: 'Mother of all editors' Emacs is 50
keyFacts: The Emacs text editor, created at the MIT AI Lab, has reached its 50-year anniversary.
Richard Stallman led bulk development starting in 1976, and MIT Technology Review stated the editor birthed the free software movement.
GNU Emacs remains in active development today, with version 31.1 having released in August.
body: No lesser authority than the MIT Technology Review says that the Emacs editor has turned 50 years old. But then, it is biased — Emacs was invented in MIT's AI lab.
Simson Garfinkel's article is simply called EMACS turns 50, but the sub-heading explains why it matters more:
"How the MIT AI Lab's text editor gave birth to the free software movement."

There are multiple timelines and accounts of the origins of Emacs, and it is not a single monolithic application. The name is an abbreviation for " E diting MAC ro S ", and the original editor for which this set of macros was developed was TECO – "Text Editor and COrrector," written by Dan Murphy in 1962. Murphy died earlier this year at the age of 83.

The inimitable Jamie Zawinski has an encyclopedic Emacs Timeline – as he mentions at the start, his interest being that he long ago maintained a fork of GNU Emacs, originally called Lucid Emacs . It's still around, under its later name XEmacs. There are a lot of forks and re-implementations of Emacs out there, and we are not going to go into all of them, or this article would become a book – one only interesting to programmer-archeologists (to use a term coined by the late great Vernor Vinge ).

As for who originally wrote those Editing Macros, though, another history has quotations from several of the people involved: On the Origin of Emacs in 1976 . (Note – some of the quotes still contain the | symbols that marked quoted text.)
This credits Lisp boffin Guy L. Steele Jr with the original work in 1975, but in it, Steele says:

"RMS is responsible for the names 'E' and 'EMACS'. RMS still deserves 99% or 99.9% or 99.99% or 99.999% of the credit for taking a package of TECO macros and turning it into the most powerful editor on the planet."

RMS is of course Richard Stallman, and the page also quotes some emails from RMS on October 23 and 31, 1976. Mind you, just a few years after the event, in a 1981 talk now preserved on the GNU website, Stallman said, "I began the development of EMACS in 1974 with an improvement to TECO". Like all the best FOSS, even in its very early stages, it was a collaborative effort – but around late October 1976 is when RMS took over the bulk of the development.

Of the many forks of Emacs over its half a century of development, some are still just about hanging on in there. When we looked up the link for XEmacs, we were surprised to see that there was a new release: XEmacs 21.5.37 "lettuce" appeared just last month. And even the forks have forks: in this case, SXEmacs , last updated in 2020.

Most of the changes in XEmacs and SXEmacs eventually made their way back upstream to GNU Emacs, which is still in active development, although as The Register reported in 2008 , RMS is no longer the primary maintainer. GNU Emacs 31.1 appeared in August.

Cards on the metaphorical table: this vulture is not an Emacs user. We have tried. A major influence was one of the Reg FOSS desk's favorite writers, Neal Stephenson, who in 1999 published an essay called In the Beginning… Was the Command Line . (It was later republished as a rather short book, but the text is still online .) In it, he says:

"In the GNU/Linux world there are two major text editing programs: the minimalist vi (known in some implementations as elvis ) and the maximalist emacs . I use emacs, which might be thought of as a thermonuclear word processor. It was created by Richard Stallman; enough said. It is written in Lisp, which is the only computer language that is beautiful. It is colossal, and yet it only edits straight ASCII text files, which is to say, no fonts, no boldface, no underlining. In other words, the engineer-hours that, in the case of Microsoft Word, were devoted to features like mail merge, and the ability to embed feature-length motion pictures in corporate memoranda, were, in the case of emacs, focused with maniacal intensity on the deceptively simple-seeming problem of editing text. If you are a professional writer–i.e., if someone else is getting paid to worry about how your words are formatted and printed–emacs outshines all other editing software in approximately the same way that the noonday sun does the stars."

Emacs is 50-plus-year-old software, and it shows. This is a huge and complicated program: decades ago, the joke was that EMACS stood for "Eight Megs And Constantly Swapping". It is not an easy program to learn. Despite lavish documentation and a built-in tutorial, this is software so old that its terminology predates microprocessors and the personal computer.

Its exhaustive manual is 804 pages long, and to pick some trivial examples, its terms for parts of the screen use “frame” to mean what’s now called a window, and “window” to mean what’s now called a pane. In the section on Keys , it discusses the Control and Meta keys. That’s a slight snag: you don’t have a Meta key, and neither do the authors of Emacs. It was a key on the now almost legendarily rare Space Cadet Keyboard, of which the Deskthority keyboard wiki says:
“It is known as the holy grail of keyboards.”

You can buy a modern replica, the Keymacs keyboard . They are hand-made in the Czech Republic, and depending on exactly what model and specifications you want, they cost from €2,998 for the Lispsaver up to €6,878 for the A624N Space Cadet .
In other words, you can have a keyboard with a real Meta key if you want, but it is going to cost you.

One of the problems with these historical terms, unfamiliar to anyone who wasn’t already programming in the 1970s, is that meanings drift. In the context of Emacs, "Meta" means Alt, or Opt on Macs . However, KDE also uses the Meta key – but what the KDE documentation calls "Meta " is the Windows key – or Command on Macs. Like most Linux folks, the GNOME documentation calls it the Super key.
Names are important. They matter. Who's right, the Emacs folks or the KDE folks? Well, neither: nobody has Meta keys any more. We have Ctrl, Alt, and Cmd/Super/Windows.

There have been valiant efforts to modernize Emacs and bring it into line with modern UI and terminology. This vulture tried to learn Aquamacs , which modernized Emacs with a native macOS UI, but sadly it's no longer maintained.

Another, which we enjoyed trying, is ErgoEmacs , which changes the key bindings and rearranges the UI into something much more like the IBM Common User Access arrangement , as used in Windows and most Linux desktops. However, it never really caught on and you need to know your way around Emacs to install it and configure it for your regional keyboard layout.

So complex is it to configure Emacs that there are multiple pre-configured distributions of Emacs, such as Doom Emacs , or the minimalist Emacs Solo . We wish someone did a "CUA-Macs" config, with ErgoEmacs integrated and able to pick up your existing keyboard config.

Come to that, the Gershwin Desktop project that we mentioned along with GhostBSD last year is in active development, and it's based around GNUstep. Maybe its developers could pick up Aquamacs, and adapt it to GNUstep.

There is a long history of such Emacs facelifts. One instance is Borland’s Sprint word-processor, one of the selling points of which was that it could emulate the user interfaces of most of the leading MS-DOS word-processors of its day (just before they all converged on IBM CUA). Before Borland acquired it, Sprint was called The Final Word , developed by musical equipment makers Mark of the Unicorn . FinalWord was based on an Emacs clone called MINCE .
The Great Rival
Another well-known Emacs distribution is Spacemacs , which adapts Emacs to have a more Vi-like user interface.

Vi is the other seminal Unix text editor, as the Stephenson quote above mentions. As this article on Origins and the Evolution of Vi & Vim notes, it too dates back to 1976. Indeed, that’s the reason we chose the year in this story: Tilde, a text editor that doesn’t work like it’s 1976 . One feature of Tilde we enjoy is that it supports use of the mouse even on the Linux console – which is the headline new feature of GNU Emacs 31.1.

Vi is very much alive and well today. GNU Emacs is based on the original source code, but Vi mainly survives as re-implementations. The recreation Stephenson mentions, Elvis, lives on today in the form of nvi .

However, by far the best known is Vim , maintained by Bram Moolenaar until his death in 2023 . In the grand FOSS forking tradition, it too has forks, including Neovim , as used in Omarchy, and more recently, the AI-free Vim Classic – a new project led by Drew DeVault, who just launched the similarly LLM-free AlpineBSD . ®

articles.headline: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
keyFacts: Neocloud firms lease high-powered computers to major AI developers, but analysts and investors have raised concerns about their heavy debt loads.
Stock prices for neocloud firms like CoreWeave and Nebius have dropped significantly over the past month amid growing financial worries.
Industry analysts predict that many neocloud firms face consolidation or acquisition as borrowing costs rise and their financial risks increase.
body: - Published
A once-obscure corner of the AI ecosystem finds itself in the spotlight â and investors don't all like what they see.
Names like CoreWeave and Nebius are familiar to the tech set in San Francisco and Silicon Valley.
These data centre companies, known as neocloud firms, run large warehouses packed with expensive computers, which they lease to major AI developers like Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta.
They're now the subject of one of Silicon Valley's most heated debates.
Many question whether neocloud firms are financially sound and what their recent stumbles tell us about the state of the AI economy.

Analysts at Gartner predict by 2030, 80% of neocloud firms will "cease independent operations", while Forrester's experts expect at least three of them to be imminently acquired "as finances get shaky".
On Thursday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tried to downplay recent concerns about neocloud firms, calling them "a small component of the overall ecosystem, external" on CNBC.
Debt worries
Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.
Firms can then borrow money using those contracts â plus the AI chips they purchase â as collateral, explained analyst Cory Johnson of "The Quiet Period" IPO research outfit.
He said debt is common across neocloud firms because the hardware has to be paid for up front.
Take the industry leader: CoreWeave. It's a fraction of the size of some of the Big Tech companies it serves.
But Johnson believes lenders sometimes consider the creditworthiness of CoreWeave's customers, like Microsoft or Meta, more than the company's when they lend.
"This helps explain how CoreWeave accumulated $35.1bn (Â£26.3bn) in debt," he said.
Some jittery investors appear to be having second thoughts.
CoreWeave stock has lost a quarter of its value over the past month, and it's not alone.
Shares in other neocloud firms like Nebius, IREN, and Applied Digital have all shed about that much if not more during the same period.
Debt investors also appear spooked, and are demanding ever-higher returns from several firms in the sector.

CoreWeave's CEO Mike Intrator has said that the market is acting "irrationally" and has expressed confidence in its business model. Some of the world's most consequential companies are queuing up for CoreWeave's infrastructure and other AI services.
Origins in crypto
Several neocloud firms have their roots in the volatile crypto mining industry, made of companies that generate cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin.
Crypto miners use some of the same kind of physical infrastructure that is used to develop AI.
CoreWeave was founded in 2017 with a focus on mining Ethereum.
IREN, Core Scientific and Applied Digital also started in crypto mining.
Their infrastructure left them well-positioned when AI exploded in 2022 with the introduction of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
One outlier is Nebius, which was known as Yandex NV when it was part of Russia's version of Google before splitting off and changing its name in 2024.
Now, the success of these firms hinges on the fate of major AI developers and hyperscalers â even larger data centre operators which neocloud firms often count as key customers.
"There is just an enormous amount of spending getting injected into the system," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global. "It's an arms race."
And neoclouds have benefitted.
But the trade-off of their model is "greater financial risk" in the face of change, said Forrester VP and principal analyst Charlie Dai.
That includes any adjustments that their Big Tech customers might make to their spending plans.
This past week, when Microsoft and Google forecast less AI spending than Wall Street analysts had projected, shares in several neocloud firms tumbled.
Much is also riding on Anthropic and OpenAI, which are both expected to start selling shares to the public in the months ahead.
If AI proves to be a bubble â and bursts â neocloud firms "are definitely going to face collateral damage," said Bradley Tusk of Tusk Ventures.
'Guppy-level death'
The future of the neoclouds also depend on their ability to keep borrowing, which gets more expensive as interest rates rise.
In a recent social media post, Elon Musk suggested this challenge could lead more than 200 neoclouds to "see guppy-level death and consolidation", with the smallest firms being the most vulnerable.
"Some will make it through, but not many," he added.
For now, analysts at Yorkville Ives said demand for computing power still exceeds supply, adding that neoclouds are filling an important gap that larger data centre companies cannot fill.
But to some, the neocloud sector's recent wobbles are concerning.
Microsoft recently cancelled a deal with a British neocloud outfit called Nscale amid power supply issues which could last through to 2030.
Australia's Firmus just shelved plans to start selling shares to the public.
These developments come amid a public backlash against data centres and questions about how much value AI can add to worker productivity.
"There's reason to worry," said Johnson.

articles.headline: November 2026 Skywatching Guide: Meteors, Planets, Stars and a Full Moon
keyFacts: All planets are visible during November, featuring an alignment of Mercury, Venus, Mars, and Jupiter between Nov. 14 and 25.
Three meteor showers peak in November, including the Southern Taurids, Northern Taurids, and Leonids.
The Beaver Moon supermoon peaks on Nov. 24, beginning a string of four consecutive supermoons that ends in 2027.
body: Autumn is marching right along, and so are the objects in the night sky. November is the final full month of fall, and with daylight saving time ending Nov. 1, the sun will set even earlier. That’ll give skygazers more time to see some cool sights without staying up horribly late or waking up unbearably early.
When to see each planet in November

Every planet is visible during the month of November, though depending on the time and day, you’ll get a better or worse view of them. Mercury and Venus are the most difficult to see due to their proximity to the sun.
More from CNET

Mercury: Mercury was at its eastern elongation during October, so it starts November a bit too close to the sun to see safely. It reaches western elongation on Nov. 20, where it’ll be easily visible just before sunrise for the rest of the month.

Venus: Venus starts the month just ahead of the sun at sunrise, technically making it possible to see every morning in November. It gets further from the sun as the month goes on, making it easier and safer to see toward the end of the month.

Mars: Mars is high in the sky all month. It rises out of the eastern horizon shortly after midnight at the start of November and rises earlier as the month progresses. Early morning is the best time to see it, or right around midnight toward the end of the month.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are close pals for all of November, rising at roughly the same time and right next to each other in the sky. The star Regulus joins in to form a trio, which is visible to the naked eye the entire month.

Saturn: Saturn is also visible every night in November. It’s in the eastern sky when the sun sets, and sets on the western horizon shortly before sunrise. Right after dark is the best time to see it, but you’ll need binoculars or a telescope to capture its glorious rings.
Neptune: Neptune and Saturn are teamed up for November, with both of them being very close in the sky and following a similar trajectory. Bring binoculars or a telescope.

Uranus: Uranus is in the night sky every day in November, rising in the east shortly before sunset and setting in the west right around sunrise. It reaches opposition on Nov. 25, which means it’s as far away from the sun as it can get, and will be the most visible. You’ll still want to bring some binoculars or a telescope for best results.
Nov. 2-3: The moon, Mars and Jupiter dance party

The month begins with a meetup among Mars, Jupiter and the moon. The three will appear close together in the night sky, making them easy to spot: The moon is easy to find, and both planets are visible to the naked eye. On Nov. 2, the moon will be closer to Mars, and the trio will follow one another across the sky throughout the night. Regulus will also be in tow and readily visible to the naked eye.

Nov. 3 continues the good vibes. The moon slides over to the other side of Regulus on that night, but all four celestial bodies are still quite close together and easy to spot. Mars, Jupiter and Regulus will get even closer to each other as November progresses, but the moon moves even further away after Nov. 3.
Nov. 4-5: Southern Taurids meteor shower peaks

The Southern Taurids have technically been active since Sept. 20, and continue until Nov. 20. This long-running meteor shower peaks during the evening of Nov. 4 and morning of Nov. 5. It’s not a terribly strong meteor shower and should average about five meteors per hour. However, it often tosses bright fireballs, so what it lacks in quantity, it makes up for in quality.

The moon is 22% illuminated that night, which the American Meteor Society calls “favorable conditions” for viewing a meteor shower. You want to get as far away from light pollution as possible to give yourself even better odds, and make sure to dress for the weather. The Southern Taurids will appear to originate from the Taurus constellation, which rises in the east shortly after sunset and moves across the sky before setting in the west right before sunrise.
Nov. 9: The best night for hunting stars

It’s no secret that the full moon is usually the most popular celestial event to happen every month, but skygazers also value the new moon. This is because the moon is a significant source of light pollution, making many stars and planets, such as Uranus and Neptune, harder to see. With the new moon on Nov. 9, it’ll be the darkest night of November — and perfect for stargazing and night-sky photography.

Nov. 9 also happens to be Carl Sagan Day, an unofficial holiday to honor the visionary astronomer. If you’re stuck inside that night, you can always use the occasion to watch Sagan’s legendary Cosmos series, which is available for free on the Internet Archive or through various user uploads on YouTube.
Nov. 14-25: A four-planet alignment

Most of the planets are visible in the night sky almost every night in November, but on Nov. 14 there’ll be a fun little planet parade. It’ll take place just before sunrise, so it’s mostly for early risers. Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter are set to line up nicely, making them easy to spot. This is especially true for Jupiter and Mars, which should be right next to each other that night.

The show will start around Nov. 14 and will last until around Nov. 25, depending on your location. The tricky part is catching Mercury in the sky before the sun comes up. It’s only about a 30-minute window since the sun closely follows Mercury up over the eastern horizon. The single best day to view it is Nov. 20, when Mercury is at its western elongation — as far from the sun as it can get.

Uranus is also visible at this time, bringing the number of visible planets to three. Saturn and Neptune are below the horizon. Uranus is on the other side of the sky, however, so it’s not technically part of the alignment.
Nov. 11-12: Northern Taurids peaks

If you miss the Southern Taurids, you only have to wait a week to catch a glimpse of the Northern Taurids meteor shower. This is another long-lasting meteor shower that started on Oct. 20 and runs until Dec. 10. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 11 and the morning of Nov. 12. The American Meteor Society notes that the moon is only 5% illuminated on Nov. 11, giving viewers even better conditions than during the Southern Taurids.

It is otherwise virtually identical to the Southern Taurids. The shower appears to originate from the same constellation, Taurus, which rises and sets at almost exactly the same times as it did a week earlier. The Northern Taurids promise about five meteors per hour under optimal conditions, with an increased chance of fireballs. Both showers are even fueled by the same comet, 2P/Encke. It’s the space equivalent of a sitcom rerun airing just one week later.
Nov. 16-17: Leonids peaks

Leonids is usually the most active meteor shower in November. It starts on Nov. 6 and runs until Nov. 30, making it shorter than both Taurids meteor showers. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 16 and the morning of Nov. 17.

The good news is that the meteor shower is very easy to find. Meteors from it will appear to originate from the Leo constellation, which is right next to Mars and Jupiter, which are visible in the night sky.

The bad news is that this part of the sky doesn’t rise until around midnight, making this a meteor shower for night owls. It should produce about 15 meteors per hour under optimal conditions, though you can expect slightly fewer because the 41%-illuminated moon will create enough natural light pollution to obscure fainter meteors.

The Leonids have produced exceptional meteor storms in the past, with hundreds of meteors per hour. That isn’t expected to happen in 2026, but the odds aren’t zero. They may improve after the comet loops around the sun again in 2031.
Nov. 23-24: Supermoon

November’s Beaver Moon takes place just two days before Thanksgiving. It is also the first of a string of four consecutive supermoons that will close out 2026 and begin 2027. This happens when the moon is within 90% of perigee — its closest point to Earth. The phenomenon makes the moon appear about 7% larger than a regular moon and 14% larger than a minimoon — and noticeably brighter than both.

Per The Old Farmer’s Almanac, the Beaver Moon reaches its peak illumination on Nov. 24 at 9:53 a.m. ET, which is after sunrise for most people in the US. That means the best time to see it is either the night before (Nov. 23) or the evening after (Nov. 24). The moon remains over 90% full from Nov. 22-27. If you plan on going skygazing, avoid those days like the plague, since the moon creates a ton of light pollution.
Nov. 30: Another moon, Mars and Jupiter dance party

It’s not often that the same event happens twice in a single month, but it turns out Jupiter, Mars and the moon just can’t seem to get enough of each other. The trio closes out the month the same way it started: hanging out very close together in the night sky. And yes, Regulus will once again tag along.

Unlike the prior meetup, this one only lasts for one night before the moon dashes away. Since all four of them are visible with the naked eye and the moon is still mostly full, people shouldn’t have any trouble finding them. Eagle-eyed stargazers may see Algieba nearby as well. It’s the second brightest star in the Leo constellation (behind Regulus), and it’s also visible without binoculars or a telescope.
All month: Constellations and asterisms

The constellations continue their summer-to-winter shakeup. Prominent constellations in the sky include Taurus, Pegasus, Capricornus, Aquila, Pisces and Aries. Mainstays such as the Big Dipper and Little Dipper are still out there, but can be difficult to see if you live too far south. As a rule, we recommend using a sky map or a tool such as Stellarium to pinpoint each object so you can find it.

There are also some lesser-known asterisms to seek out, such as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters), the Great Square of Pegasus and the Circlet of Pisces. The Summer Triangle is still visible, while the Winter Triangle becomes much easier to spot as it rises above the horizon earlier in the evening.

articles.headline: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
keyFacts: A new Science study shows that Manx shearwaters experience jet lag when they fly across time zones over the North Atlantic.
Researchers said that because these seabirds navigate using the Sun, their jet lag skews their internal compass.
Patrick Lewin and other researchers explained that effective solar navigation requires an internal clock, but the birds' clock is imperfect.
body: Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it’s the middle of the night while the clock says it’s lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans.

A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass.
Clockwork compass

Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales.

From there, they head out to feed anywhere from a few dozen to more than 1,000 kilometers into the Atlantic. To get back, shearwaters are thought to work out where they are located using a map sense, possibly based on smells, and then use the Sun as a compass to set their direction.

The trouble with navigating by the Sun, though, is that it moves across the sky. “You can imagine an animal or a human that wants to travel south all day. At sunrise, when the Sun’s in the east, it needs to be traveling 90 degrees clockwise of the Sun, but by midday it needs to be traveling straight towards the Sun, and by sunset it needs to be traveling 90 degrees anticlockwise of the Sun,” Lewin said. Effective navigation by the Sun requires a clock that tells you what time of day it is. Birds, like nearly all animals, have such a clock built in. But the clock in Manx shearwaters is not perfect.
